figure_alt.Z14-P55: Left: a dial gauge with a 0 to 20 pound scale. An untested gauge reads 11 pounds while the true canner pressure is 9 pounds; a gauge that reads high causes under-processing. Dial gauges are checked for accuracy each year before use, adjusted when off by up to 2 pounds and replaced when off by more. Right: a weighted gauge on the vent pipe rocks or jiggles as the maker describes and needs no accuracy check; above 1,000 feet the tested table calls for the next heavier weight. Conceptual, not to scale.
figure_alt.Z14-P56: Pressure-versus-time trace for a pressure canner. Pressure rises to the target, holds, then dips below the target for a short time before it is restored. Below the trace, adding the lost minutes at the end is crossed out; the full process time restarts from the moment target pressure returns. A note applies the same rule to a boiling-water canner when the boil stops. Conceptual, not to scale.
figure_alt.Z14-P57: Left: the same pot of water boiling at sea level and at a higher elevation; water boils at a lower temperature as altitude increases, and lower boiling temperatures are less effective at killing bacteria, so sea-level settings can under-process at 1,000 feet or more. Right: the tested recipe has separate tables for boiling-water, dial-gauge and weighted-gauge canners; at higher elevation the boiling-water time increases, the dial-gauge pressure increases, and the weighted gauge moves to the next heavier weight. Values are never moved between tables. Conceptual, not to scale.
figure_alt.Z14-P53: Cross-section of an atmospheric steam canner: a shallow base holds water under a rack of jars, steam fills the dome and air is vented out before timing begins. Limits: acid or properly acidified foods with pH 4.6 or below, a total process of 45 minutes or less including altitude adjustment, and no opening to add water during processing. It is not a pressure canner and is not used for low-acid foods. Conceptual, not to scale.
figure_alt.Z14-P48: Left: jars processed in a conventional oven, open-kettle filling with jars turned upside down, a microwave oven, a dishwasher and a paraffin wax seal are each crossed out; USDA does not recommend them because they do not prevent all risks of spoilage. Right: a boiling-water canner with water over the jar tops and a pressure canner holding at least four quart jars, used with a tested recipe. Conceptual, not to scale.
